articleTitle: Maximum power transfer capabilities of electrical transmission systems
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The maximum power transfer capability of an uncompensated electrical transmission system can easily be determined for any desired voltage drop between the sending and receiving end of a system but If shunt or series capitance is added the voltage drop can be kept to any desired limit and it becomes necessary to establish further criteria before the maximum transfer capability can be established. This paper gives a brief review of general power transfer theory and then investigates and suggests general criteria which can be used to establish maximum transfer capabilities of practical transmission systems using reactive compensation. These criteria are then used to derive general results which are presented In the form of curves giving maximum power angles, power transfer capabilities and reactive compensation requirements for any value of the system impedance angle. Thermal and economic limits are then considered and the restrictions Imposed by static and transient stability considerations are briefly discussed.

articleTitle: The future of telecommunications
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This lecture depicts the likely developments in telecommunications during the next half century. The main overland and submarine information highways will consist of wideband optical quadratic-law fibres with laser-type repeaters spaced just over 2 km apart. Local-area distribution will be based on narrower band glass fibres with a fibre information rate of the order of 300 megabits/sec as opposed to the 10 to 20 gigabits/sec per fibre on the main highways. Switching will use both time and space switches employing advanced optical techniques. The whole network will use digital techniques and lasers throughout. Holographic crystal stores using lasers for writing and reading will be located at strategic points. Standard subscriber's equipment will include video cameras and receivers, crystal stores, play-back devices, and terminals for communicating with computers, banks, shopping centres, etc. Mobile telephone services will be universal and will employ revolutionary techniques. Free space radio will be restricted almost entirely to mobile services. Pocket telephones and global personal telephone numbers will be commonplace. Information retrieval centres will replace central libraries. Aircraft and ships will employ earth satellites for communication and navigation on an extensive scale, while similar services to space vehicles in the solar system will be highly developed.

articleTitle: Power System Planning Techniques Current United States Practices
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In the United States, as in many other world areas, the availability of a reliable, high-quality supply of electric energy is taken for granted. Today, the customer expects to connect his alarm clock, his computer or his industrial plant and obtain a continuous supply of electrical energy at standard voltage and frequency. Living up to these standards Is the major challenge for the modern electric utility. With today's mammoth interconnections composed of individual utilities, power pools, super-pools or regional interconnections interlacing over thousands of miles it is essential to resort to the assistance of large-scale computer programmes for system planning purposes. Studies typically undertaken with the aid of computers include load prediction, generation expansion, production costing, transmission expansion, load flow and stability studies.

abstract: At the time it was planned in 1964, the South Africa-Portugal submarine telephone cable, which would provide the highest number of channels over the longest distance yet attempted, was the most comprehensive project of its kind. A description of the cable, submerged repeaters and equalisers and the terminal and power equipment then precedes sections on the survey of the route, the laying of the cable and the installation of the terminal and power equipment. On completion of the acceptance tests and the overall commissioning, the system was officially opened for service on the 18th February, 1969, by the Honourable B. J. articleTitle: Insulating oil in relation to the maintenance of power transformers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper reviews the present state of knowledge regarding oil/paper dielectrics and analyses the factors that reduce service life. It is found that insulating oil in contact with air absorbs oxygen which attacks hydrocarbon molecules under the Influence of heat, producing the well-known oxidation products — organic acids and sludge. Organic acid has long been considered a major contaminant of transformer oil. But research and experience indicate that its most harmful effects are not the erosion of metals below oil level, which is negligible, nor the degradation of oil and paper insulation but Its effect in raising the hygroscopy of oil. Although humidity has practically no effect on oil oxidation, an Increase in oil's affinity for water accelerates the absorption and transfer of moisture from air in contact with the oil to the extremely hygroscopic paper insulation immersed in it. The combined effects of temperature, oxygen and humidity lead to polymerisation of oil and oxidation products, and decomposition of paper insulation leading to the eventual breakdown of a transformer in service. Modern methods of conditioning and testing insulating oil, as well as the economics of oil purification, are reviewed.

articleTitle: Process control and other fields of automation
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The basic principles involved in control by digital computer are discussed with special reference to the mathematical model, optimization and the breakdown of costs. Expected future developments are briefly mentioned. A few case histories are given of computer control in South Africa. Automation is illustrated with reference to a few industries such as steel, power generation and tobacco, also its application in the fields of transport, postal services and broadcasting; special reference is made to what has been done in South Africa. Computer-aided design and computer graphics are briefly mentioned. The importance of numerically controlled machine tools for South Africa is dealt with and a summary of the present application in South Africa is given. The Implications of small-scale automation for South Africa are also discussed. Steps already taken to promote and plan for automation in South Africa are mentioned; reference is made to sociological problems and the possible use of unskilled labour. The extent of the present market for automation and control systems equipment in South Africa is estimated.
